name: Ben Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dozer operator at the Redgum bauxite mine, a big open-cut operation, and I lead the dozer crew on days. We push overburden, the soil and rock on top of the ore, build the ramps and clean up behind the shovels. For the last year I've also been running one of our two remote-control dozers from a cabin at the edge of the pit, which I put my hand up for. I like the problem-solving, working out how to shape a slope in the fewest passes, and I don't love the vibration, which my back is starting to complain about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, probably more than most people on site. I use an AI assistant every morning to go over the survey data and plan the push sequence, and I've got a drone licence on the side. My partner Kate is a bookkeeper, and she says I spend more time reading about autonomous machines than watching TV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold. I'd probably say it on the forum I'm on, where a lot of us operators argue about this stuff. Most people would be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd keep using the tools for planning, keep doing the remote dozer, and my skills would still count for something. The extra skills just make me a bit more valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning, and probably grow my drone survey work on weekends, because farmers and builders around town pay for it. Maybe 300 a month extra. Savings stay where they are, about four months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone work. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend's farm needed a dam surveyed and the surveyor wanted two grand. I'd just got my licence, so I did it for a case of beer and a barbecue. Now I've got a dozen paying clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a quiet AI world change your plans for the dozer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The back's the bigger issue. Remote dozing is easier on the body, so I'd push to do more of that whether the AI hype is real or not.

S0.say: I'd say on my operators' forum that AI is a useful tool that got oversold. Most people would be quietly pleased.
S0.think: Privately I'd be fine, because I'd keep the planning tools and the remote dozer. The extra skills just make me a bit more valuable.
S0.do: Keeps working and learning, and grows his weekend drone survey work for local farmers and builders by about 300 a month. Keeps roughly four months of savings and pushes to do more remote dozing for his back.
S0.quote: I'd just got my licence, so I did it for a case of beer and a barbecue. Now I've got a dozen paying clients.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is already ahead on technology and has a small drone survey business on the side. His biggest physical worry is his back, which also pushes him toward remote work. A quiet AI world suits him fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and the smart move is to get on board early. I'd say it to the crew and on the forum. I'd also say the company should train everybody, not just the keen ones like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. Someone has to run the remote dozers and plan the work for autonomous machines, and I'm already doing it. I might end up with a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the mine to put me on the autonomous systems team properly, and do whatever certificates they offer. I'd put some savings into a better drone and a mapping software licence, maybe five grand. And I'd teach two or three of my crew the remote dozer so they're not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some excitement. A bit of worry for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five grand out of four months of savings is a real chunk. Why risk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the drone work is the one bit of income nobody can roster me off. If the mine changes, I want something that's mine. Kate checked the numbers and she's okay with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, mainly. He's 57, the best dozer man I've ever seen on a wet slope, but he can't stand screens. I'd try to get him on the training, but I don't know if he'd stick it.

S1.say: I'd say to the crew and the forum that it's happening and the smart move is to get on board early. The company should train everybody, not just keen ones like me.
S1.think: Privately I think this is good for me, because someone has to run the remote dozers and plan for autonomous machines. I might end up with a better job.
S1.do: Asks to join the mine's autonomous systems team and takes any certificates offered. Spends about five grand of savings on a better drone and mapping software, and trains a few crew members on the remote dozer.
S1.feel: Calm with some excitement and some worry for the crew.
S1.quote: The drone work is the one bit of income nobody can roster me off.
S1.fieldNote: Ben sees steady disruption as a chance and is willing to spend a real share of his savings on his side business. His pragmatism shows in checking the numbers with his partner first. He worries about an older crew member who avoids screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock and the government will need to do something for people fast, some kind of income support, at least for a while. I'd also say people should learn to use the new systems because some jobs will be around them for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even my remote job goes. If AI can do any work, it can plan a push sequence and drive a dozer. My edge is a couple of years at most, and the drone surveys would get automated too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the drone business straight away and keep the cash. I'd try to get onto the team installing the autonomous fleet, because that's the last people job before it runs itself. We'd cut back at home, skip the holiday, and I'd talk to Kate about her bookkeeping, since that's exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it's not fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been ahead of the curve. Does two years of warning still help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd get maybe a year or two more work than someone who never touched it. But being early to a party that ends at midnight only gets you so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kate's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that worries me most, honestly. Bookkeeping is exactly what AI is good at. If we both go in the same year, four months of savings is nothing.

S2.say: I'd say it's a big shock and the government needs to provide income support fast, at least for a while. People should still learn the new systems because some jobs will be around them briefly.
S2.think: Privately I think even my remote job goes, because AI could plan and drive the dozer itself. My edge is a couple of years at most, and the drone surveys would go too.
S2.do: Stops spending on the drone business and holds cash. Tries to join the team installing the autonomous fleet, cuts back at home and skips the holiday, and talks with his partner about her exposed bookkeeping job.
S2.feel: Anxious, not panicking, but not enjoying it.
S2.quote: Being early to a party that ends at midnight only gets you so much.
S2.fieldNote: Ben is clear-eyed that his head start shrinks to a year or two under a fast timeline. His sharpest worry is his partner's bookkeeping job, since both incomes could fall at once. He stays in control but knows the limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell my crew to learn the systems and save money. I'd say the government should help pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay for most of those five years, maybe all of them. I'd be one of the people setting it up. After that, I'm not sure, but I'd have money and contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the autonomous fleet work at the mine, and I'd use the drone side to learn about inspection work, which might last longer. We'd pay the mortgage down harder and aim for eight months of savings. Kate would probably move into advising small businesses instead of just doing their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More uneasy than the slow one, less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between two and five years for you, in plain terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'm hanging on. With five I can actually build something. It's enough time to make some money from the change before it finishes the job off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel any guilt being in a better position than your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. Mick wouldn't make it, and I know it. I'd push the company to pay him out properly, that's the least they can do.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell my crew to learn the systems and save, and the government should help pay for retraining.
S3.think: I'd be okay for most of the five years as one of the people setting it up. After that I'm not sure, but I'd have money and contacts.
S3.do: Goes all in on the mine's autonomous fleet work and uses the drone side to learn inspection work. Pays the mortgage down harder, aims for eight months of savings, and supports his partner moving into small business advice.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more than in the steady picture but less than in the fast one.
S3.quote: It's enough time to make some money from the change before it finishes the job off.
S3.fieldNote: Ben expects to profit during the transition and is frank that it ends eventually. He admits some guilt about his older colleague and wants the company to pay him out fairly. His household plans include his partner changing work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell young operators to treat it like an apprenticeship for the next thing. I'd say that on the forum and to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53. I think I'd be fine. I'd probably end up running a small inspection or survey business, using the robots instead of competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the next few years I'd grow the drone business into a proper company, maybe buy a couple of robotic survey units once they're cheap. I'd stay at the mine on the autonomous side as long as it pays well. We'd put money into the business and keep paying the house down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Using robots instead of competing with them. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say a mine or a farm needs a site checked every week. I'd own the machines that do it, and I'd sell the result, not my hours. That's the trick, own the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's enough work for anyone, in the end. If everybody's got robots, who's paying for surveys? I don't know the answer, and I don't think anyone does.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell young operators to treat it like an apprenticeship for what comes next.
S4.think: At 53 I think I'd be fine, probably running a small inspection or survey business. I'd use the robots instead of competing with them.
S4.do: Grows the drone work into a proper company over a few years and buys robotic survey units once they're cheap. Stays on the mine's autonomous side while it pays and keeps paying down the house.
S4.quote: I'd own the machines that do it, and I'd sell the result, not my hours.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Ben plans to become an owner of automation rather than a worker replaced by it. He is honest that he doesn't know whether there will be enough demand in the end. His centre politics show in wanting some public help while backing his own enterprise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Kate. My job I can scramble with, but both of us at once with two kids is the scary bit. What would help is short, cheap courses that actually lead to jobs, and some income support that kicks in quickly, not after six months of forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who ends up owning the robots. If it's only the big companies, most of us are just renting our lives back from them. I'd want small operators like me to be able to buy in.

headlineQuote: My job I can scramble with, but both of us at once with two kids is the scary bit.
portrait: Ben Weber is a 43-year-old dozer crew lead at the Redgum bauxite mine who already runs a remote-control dozer, uses AI daily to plan his work and runs a weekend drone survey business. He lives with his partner Kate, a bookkeeper, and their two kids, with a mortgage and about four months saved. He sees steady change as a chance and would spend savings on his side business, but in the two-year AGI picture he worries most that his and Kate's jobs could go at once. With five or ten years he plans to own the machines rather than compete with them.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he and his partner could both lose their jobs at the same time with two children to support.
whatWouldHelp: Short, cheap courses that lead to real jobs, and income support that starts quickly rather than after months of forms.
